questions.concept: Memory process sequence: Encoding → Storage → Retrieval

questions.question:

questions.question:
Match the items of List-I with those of List-II:

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| (A) Continuity | (i) tendency to perceive a whole object even where none exists |
| (B) Common fate | (ii) objects in motion together appear to stand out from their surroundings |
| (C) Proximity | (iii) elements that continue a pattern are likely to be seen as part of the pattern |
| (D) Closure | (iv) elements found close together tend to be perceived as a unit |

**Codes:**

| | (A) | (B) | (C) | (D) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | (i) | (ii) | (iii) | (iii) |
| (B) | (iv) | (iv) | (i) | (ii) |
| (C) | (ii) | (i) | (ii) | (iv) |
| (D) | (iii) | (iii) | (iv) | (i) |
questions.concept: Gestalt perceptual organization principles: Continuity = elements that continue a pattern are likely to be seen as part of the pattern (iii). Common fate = objects in motion together appear to stand out from their surroundings (ii). Proximity = elements found close together tend to be perceived as a unit (iv). Closure = tendency to perceive a whole object even where none exists (i). Option (A) correctly maps A=iii, B=ii, C=iv, D=i.
questions.explanation: A=iii (Continuity: elements continuing a pattern are seen as part of it), B=ii (Common fate: objects moving together stand out), C=iv (Proximity: elements close together perceived as a unit), D=i (Closure: tendency to perceive whole object). Option (A) now correctly reflects this mapping.

questions.question: Nature of intelligence is like electricity which is easy to measure but difficult to define. Who advocated this view?
questions.concept: Binet's pragmatic view: intelligence is like electricity — measurable but hard to define

questions.question:
Arrange the following processes in order in which they occur in test construction:

(I) Item analysis
(II) Validity
(III) Reliability
(IV) Norms
questions.concept: Test construction sequence: Item analysis → Reliability → Validity → Norms (reliability is prerequisite for validity; test cannot be valid without being reliable)

questions.question: Which two processes are always involved in perception?
questions.concept: Perception always involves sensation and interpretation (same as Q17 — duplicate question in original paper)

questions.question:
Valid theory of motivation accounts for:

(I) Innate tendencies for action
(II) Tension reduction and equilibrium
(III) Growth and development of behaviour
(IV) Arousal, selectivity and direction of behaviour
questions.concept: A comprehensive theory of motivation must account for innate biological tendencies (instinct/drive theories) AND growth/development of behaviour (humanistic theories). Tension reduction (II) and arousal/selectivity/direction (IV) are also important but per UGC key, I and III are the required elements. [Verify against official answer key if available.]

questions.question:
Match List-I (Theorist) with List-II (Concept of Intelligence):

| List-I (Theorist) | List-II (Concept of Intelligence) |
|---|---|
| (A) Cattel | (i) A triarchic theory of Intelligence |
| (B) Spearman | (ii) Seven independent mental ability |
| (C) Sternberg | (iii) Two clusters of Mental abilities |
| (D) Thurstone | (iv) Intelligence is g factor |

**Codes:**

| | (A) | (B) | (C) | (D) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | (ii) | (iii) | (i) | (iii) |
| (B) | (i) | (iv) | (ii) | (iv) |
| (C) | (iii) | (i) | (iv) | (i) |
| (D) | (iv) | (ii) | (iii) | (ii) |
questions.concept: Intelligence theorists and their contributions: Cattell proposed two clusters of mental abilities — fluid (Gf) and crystallized (Gc) intelligence (iii). Spearman proposed the two-factor theory with a general intelligence factor or g factor (iv). Sternberg developed the triarchic theory of intelligence encompassing analytical, creative, and practical abilities (i). Thurstone proposed seven independent primary mental abilities including verbal comprehension, word fluency, number facility, spatial visualization, associative memory, perceptual speed, and reasoning (ii). Option (D) correctly maps A=iii, B=iv, C=i, D=ii.
questions.explanation: A=iii (Cattell: two clusters of mental abilities — fluid and crystallized), B=iv (Spearman: g factor or general intelligence), C=i (Sternberg: triarchic theory — analytical, creative, practical), D=ii (Thurstone: seven independent primary mental abilities). Option (D) now correctly reflects this mapping.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is not correct?
options: (A) Group factor theory of intelligence is associated with Thurstone
(B) Multifactor theory of intelligence was propounded by Thorndike
(C) Multi-Dimensional structure of intellect was developed by Guilford
(D) Two factor theory of intelligence was proposed by Vernon
questions.correct_text: Two factor theory of intelligence was proposed by Vernon
questions.concept: INCORRECT statement (D): Two factor theory was proposed by Spearman, not Vernon. Thurstone IS correctly associated with group factor theory (Primary Mental Abilities). Vernon proposed Hierarchical theory.

questions.question:
A continuous reinforcement schedule is:

(I) effective for strengthening a new response
(II) a fixed-interval schedule
(III) a procedure involving reinforcement of each occurrence of a desired response
(IV) a fixed-ratio schedule

Which of the following is true?
options: (B) I, II and III are correct
(C) I, III and IV are correct
(D) I, II, III and IV are correct
questions.concept: Continuous reinforcement (CRF) schedule: (I) It is effective for strengthening a new response — true, as reinforcing every instance of a new behavior helps establish it quickly. (III) It is a procedure involving reinforcement of each occurrence of a desired response — true, this is the definition of CRF. Statements II and IV are false: CRF is NOT a fixed-interval schedule (which reinforces after a set time period) and NOT a fixed-ratio schedule (which reinforces after a set number of responses). CRF and partial reinforcement schedules are distinct categories. Option (A) correctly identifies only I and III.
questions.explanation: I and III only: CRF reinforces every response (III), making it effective for new responses (I). CRF is neither a fixed-interval nor fixed-ratio schedule — those are partial/intermittent reinforcement schedules. Option (A) now correctly states 'I and III only'.

questions.question: In classical conditioning, the time interval between CS and UCS is an important determinant of the strength of conditioning. Which of the following statements is true in respect of such temporal arrangement?
options: (A) Longer intervals lead to better recognition of the CS.
(B) Simultaneous presentation of CS and UCS is necessary for conditioning to occur.
(C) Short intervals result in early extinction.
(D) Extremely short intervals of less than 0.2 second rarely produce conditioning
questions.correct_text: Extremely short intervals of less than 0.2 second rarely produce conditioning
questions.concept: CS-UCS interval: too short (<0.2s) prevents conditioning; optimal is ~0.5s delay

Match theories of intelligence (List-I) with their conceptualization (List-II):

| List-I | List-II |

| (A) Gardner's Theory | (i) Intelligence is a basic processing mechanism |
| (B) Anderson's Theory | (ii) Each mental activity involves an operation on some kind of content that results in some product |
| (C) Ceci's Bioecological Theory | (iii) Intelligence is an ability to solve problems |
| (D) Guilford's Theory | (iv) Intelligence involves multiple cognitive potentials that are biologically based |

**Codes:**

| | (A) | (B) | (C) | (D) |
|---|---|---|---|---|

| (B) | (iv) | (i) | (i) | (iii) |

Anderson's theory posits that intelligence is a basic processing mechanism underlying all cognitive activity (i). Ceci's bioecological theory holds that intelligence involves multiple cognitive potentials that are biologically based and shaped by environmental context (iv). Guilford's Structure of Intellect model proposes that each mental activity involves an operation on some kind of content that results in some product (ii). Option (A) correctly maps A=iii, B=i, C=iv, D=ii.

Option (A) now correctly reflects this mapping.

questions.question:
Match the List-I with List-II:

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| (A) Cannon-Bard | (i) physical reactions come before experiencing emotions |
| (B) Schachter-Singer | (ii) emotions and bodily responses occur simultaneously |
| (C) James-Lange | (iii) emotional experience depends on perception of a given situation |
| (D) Tomkins | (iv) the feedback from facial expressions cause or intensify the experience of emotions |

**Codes:**

| | (A) | (B) | (C) | (D) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | (i) | (ii) | (iii) | (iv) |
| (B) | (ii) | (iii) | (iv) | (i) |
| (C) | (iv) | (iv) | (ii) | (ii) |
| (D) | (iii) | (i) | (i) | (i) |
questions.concept: Major emotion theories: Cannon-Bard theory states that emotions and bodily responses occur simultaneously — the thalamus sends signals to both the cortex (emotion) and the autonomic nervous system (bodily arousal) at the same time (ii). Schachter-Singer (two-factor) theory proposes that emotional experience depends on cognitive appraisal of a given situation — labeling physiological arousal based on environmental context (iii). James-Lange theory argues that physical reactions come before experiencing emotions — we feel sad because we cry, not cry because we feel sad (i). Tomkins' facial feedback hypothesis states that feedback from facial expressions causes or intensifies the experience of emotions — the act of smiling can make one feel happier (iv). Option (C) correctly maps A=ii, B=iii, C=i, D=iv.
questions.explanation: A=ii (Cannon-Bard: emotions and bodily responses occur simultaneously), B=iii (Schachter-Singer: emotional experience depends on cognitive appraisal), C=i (James-Lange: physical reactions precede emotional experience), D=iv (Tomkins: facial feedback causes/intensifies emotion). Option (C) now correctly reflects this mapping.

Match List-I with List-II:

| List-I (Phenomena) | List-II (Concept/Principle in operant conditioning) |
|---|---|
| (A) More preferred activity used to reinforce less preferred one | (i) Conditioned reinforcer |
| (B) Withdrawal of an aversive state following a response | (ii) Positive reinforcement |
| (C) Introduction of an aversive state following a response | (iii) Premack Principle |
| (D) Events acting as positive reinforcers through their association with primary reinforcers | (iv) Punishment |
| | (v) Negative reinforcement |

**Codes:**

| | (A) | (B) | (C) | (D) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | (i) | (iii) | (i) | (v) |
| (B) | (v) | (v) | (iv) | (iv) |
| (C) | (ii) | (iv) | (v) | (iii) |
| (D) | (iii) | (i) | (ii) | (i) |
questions.concept: Key operant conditioning concepts: (A) The Premack Principle states that a more preferred activity can be used to reinforce a less preferred one — e.g., allowing play after homework (iii). (B) Negative reinforcement involves the withdrawal or removal of an aversive state following a response, which increases the likelihood of that response recurring (v). (C) Punishment involves the introduction of an aversive state following a response, which decreases the likelihood of that response (iv). (D) A conditioned reinforcer is an event that acts as a positive reinforcer through its association with primary reinforcers — e.g., money becomes reinforcing because it is associated with obtaining food and shelter (i). Option (C) correctly maps A=iii, B=v, C=iv, D=i.
questions.explanation: A=iii (Premack Principle: more preferred activity reinforces less preferred), B=v (Negative reinforcement: withdrawal of aversive state), C=iv (Punishment: introduction of aversive state), D=i (Conditioned reinforcer: associated with primary reinforcers). Option (C) now correctly reflects this mapping.

**Assertion (A):** Variable-ratio schedule of reinforcement results in responses which are highly resistant to extinction.

**Reason (R):** When reinforcement is infrequent and intermittent, organisms continue to respond because they cannot recognize the nonavailability of reinforcement.

questions.question: Perceptual process involves:
questions.concept: Perception involves visualization, feeling, organization, and interpretation of stimuli

content.heading: Read the following passage carefully and answer questions from 45 to 50:
content.text:
With the growing interest in organizational factors in memory, it was perhaps inevitable that psychologists would turn to the analysis of mnemonic devices. Mnemonic devices are those which enable the person to enrich or elaborate upon the material to be learned, all with the aim of helping her to remember it better. They typically help the person to classify and organize the material.

One mnemonic device that has been analyzed extensively (Bower, 1970 b) is the "pegword" method for learning ordered lists of items such as shopping lists, errands, historical events, sets of laws in psychology, and so on. The person first learns a list of rhyming pegwords, pairing concrete images with the first 20 or so integers. In learning a new list of items, the person then uses successive pegwords as imagined pegs upon which to hook the successive items of the list. As the first list word occurs (cigar), the person is to call to mind her first pegword and form a mental image of some vivid scene of interaction between the two objects.

The images may be as bizarre as one wishes — their effectiveness seems independent of that aspect. This same procedure for imaginal pairing is followed for each of the list words in turn. To revive the list in memory the person needs only to go through her already well learned list of pegwords, and as she considers each one in turn she tries to recreate or recall the imaginal scene elaborated around that pegword image; from this remembered scene, she can usually name the desired item ("cigar").

This and similar schemes are exceedingly effective, at least in comparison to normal free recall of subjects not thought to use any special tricks. One of the main reasons the device works so well is that the person has a systematic retrieval scheme — she knows how to cue herself with the items (the pegwords) to which she has explicitly associated the list words as they were presented. The usual free-recall subject, on the other hand, simply does not know how to remind herself of all the list words she knows. The advantage for the pegword user, therefore, is partly the result of her knowing how to systematically retrieve each of the words from each input-list position. The second advantage of the pegword method undoubtedly stems from its deployment of mnemonic imagery.

questions.question: This passage is primarily concerned with:
options: (A) organization of memory in human brain
questions.concept: Mnemonic devices as strategies for improving memory

questions.question: The "pegword" method involves:
options: (A) using some rhyming words in sequence to associate with the words in a list to be memorised.
(C) using numbers to remember a list
(D) using rhymes to organize the words.
questions.correct_text: using some rhyming words in sequence to associate with the words in a list to be memorised.
questions.concept: Pegword method: rhyming pegwords paired with items via imagery

questions.question:
**Assertion (A):** Effective use of mnemonic devices improves recall quite significantly.

**Reason (R):** Mnemonic devices provide effective cues for retrieval.
options: (A) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
(B) Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questions.correct_text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.concept: Mnemonics improve recall by providing systematic retrieval cues

questions.question:
Mnemonic devices are:

(I) useful to learner
(II) strategies for deciding on the order of free recall
(III) the ones which provide retrieval schemes
options: (D) I, II and III are correct
questions.concept: Mnemonics are useful (I) and provide retrieval schemes (III); they're not about ordering free recall (II)

questions.question: A retrieval scheme is:
options: (A) a plan for the order of recall
(B) one way of reminding the learner of the item to be recalled
questions.correct_text: one way of reminding the learner of the item to be recalled
questions.concept: Retrieval scheme: systematic way to cue recall of learned items

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is/are true of pegword device?

(I) The nature of images do not affect the effectiveness of pegword technique.
(II) It provides the learner necessary cues to systematically recall items.
(III) The advantages of the device are due to the use of mnemonic imagery.
options: (D) I, II and III are true.
questions.correct_text: I, II and III are true.
questions.concept: Pegword: image nature doesn't matter (I), provides systematic cues (II), advantages from mnemonic imagery (III)
